3.5.1 Green’s Functions

Definition 3.5.1.1 (Green's Functions).

A Green’s function is a function of the form 𝐴−1 where 𝐴 is an operator. A standard way to evaluate these green function operators is via a Fourier transform into 𝑘-space1. This is a type of propagator.

Definition 3.5.1.2 (Propagator).

Defines or is used to define how a field propagates via applying the propagator Π to some other field or current. Can be used perturbatively in order to describe more complicated fields.

  • An example of a propagator is the 2-point Green’s function Π=−1□ which is defined by

    □𝑥Π(𝑥,𝑦)=−𝛿4(𝑥−𝑦)

  • With □𝑥=𝑔𝜇𝜈𝜕𝜕𝑥𝜇𝜕𝜕𝑥𝜈 This gives the solution (via the Fourier transform), that

    Π(𝑥,𝑦)=∫d4𝑘(2𝜋)4𝑒𝑖𝑘(𝑥−𝑦)1𝑘2
    .

===Fourier Transform of Operators Under Fourier Transforms, certain operators are effectively interchangeable with some counterpart that often simplifies calculations. An example of this is how Π(𝑥,𝑦) is interchangeable with 1𝑘2.

Example 3.5.1.3 (Delta Functions).

For an instance of this occurrence, we can utilize delta functions.

The Fourier transform of any delta function is

𝛿̃(𝑘⃗)=1⟹𝛿(𝑥⃗)=∫d3𝑘(2𝜋)3𝑒𝑖𝑘⃗⋅𝑥⃗
  • △𝑛𝛿3(𝑥⃗)=∫d3𝑘(2𝜋)3△𝑛𝑒𝑖𝑘⃗⋅𝑥⃗=∫d3𝑘(2𝜋)3(−𝑘⃗2)𝑛𝑒𝑖𝑘⃗⋅𝑥⃗

  • △𝑛⟷(−𝑘⃗2)𝑛 (this means that in a Fourier Transform, these are interchangeable).

  • Additionally, we can do the same for the relativistic □=𝜕𝜇𝜕𝜇

    □𝑛(𝛿4(𝑥))=∫d4𝑘(2𝜋)4□𝑛𝑒𝑖𝑘⋅𝑥=∫d4𝑘(2𝜋)4(−𝑘2)𝑛𝑒𝑖𝑘⋅𝑥

  • Have that [□𝑛𝛿4]̃(𝑘)=(−𝑘2)𝑛 and [△𝑛𝛿3]̃(𝑘)=(−𝑘⃗2)𝑛

3.5.2 Perturbation Theory

Definition 3.5.2.1 (Perturbation Theory).

This topic is introduced in Quantum mechanics (and often before-hand) where we consider an initial state that we can solve and then higher order terms that we continue to be able to solve. Perturbation theory only works when the leading term is the “dominant” force in play. Often, we can utilize an initial term which is non-interacting and extra terms that are interacting.

Example 3.5.2.2 (Gravity).

This example was provided from the Schwartz textbook2 We start with the Lagrangian

ℒ︀=−12ℎ□ℎ+13𝜆ℎ3+𝐽ℎ

where 𝐽 is some current and ℎ is our field. From the Euler-Lagrange equations, our equation of motion is

□ℎ−𝜆ℎ2−𝐽=0

First order approx (𝜆=0): ℎ0=1□𝐽. We let ℎ=ℎ0+ℎ1.

□(ℎ0+ℎ1)−𝜆(ℎ0+ℎ1)2−𝐽=0

implies

□ℎ1=𝜆ℎ02+𝒪︀(𝜆2)ℎ=1□𝐽+𝜆1□((1□𝐽)(1□𝐽))+𝒪︀(𝜆2)
which we now have in terms of our Green’s Functions.

In fact, something being defined as 1□𝐽 is not that uncommon, as it also happens with the Electromagnetic field.

3.5.3 OFPT

  • For Old Fashioned Perturbation Theory we utilize perturbation by setting the Hamiltonian to

    𝐻=𝐻0+𝑉

  • The idea is that we have some |𝜙⟩ and some |𝜓⟩ such that

    𝐻0|𝜙⟩=𝐸|𝜙⟩

    and

    𝐻|𝜓⟩=𝐸|𝜓⟩

  • From this we can derive

    |𝜓⟩=|𝜙⟩+1𝐸−𝐻0𝑉|𝜙⟩,

    the Lippmann-Schwinger equation

    • This allows us to define the propagator3

      ΠLS≡1𝐸−𝐻0

  • We define an operator 𝑇 as

    𝑉|𝜓⟩=𝑇|𝜙⟩|𝜓⟩=|𝜙⟩+ΠLS𝑇|𝜙⟩𝑉|𝜓⟩=𝑉|𝜙⟩+𝑉ΠLS𝑇|𝜙⟩

    • Note that 𝑉|𝜓⟩=𝑇|𝜙⟩ so

      𝑇|𝜙⟩=𝑉|𝜙⟩+𝑉ΠLS𝑇|𝜙⟩=(𝑉+𝑉ΠLS𝑇)|𝜙⟩.
      (This holds when contracted with any eigenstate of 𝐻0, |𝜙𝑗⟩)

  • This implies that that 𝑇=𝑉+𝑉ΠLS𝑇.

  • Recursion provides

    𝑇=𝑉+𝑉ΠLS𝑉+𝑉ΠLS𝑉ΠLS𝑉+⋯

If we want a transition amplitude for this, we want to calculate

⟨𝑓|𝑇|𝑖⟩=⟨𝑓|𝑉|𝑖⟩+⟨𝑓|𝑉ΠLS𝑉|𝑖⟩+⋯

  • We can insert the eigenstates within this equation due to the fact that

    ∑𝑗|𝜙𝑗⟩⟨𝜙𝑗|=𝟙

This provides

⟨𝜙𝑓|𝑇|𝜙𝑖⟩=⟨𝜙𝑓|𝑉|𝜙𝑖⟩+⟨𝜙𝑓|𝑉ΠLS|𝜙𝑗⟩⟨𝜙𝑗|𝑉|𝜙𝑖⟩+⋯

  • In an alternative/more convenient notation,

    𝑇𝑓𝑖=𝑉𝑓𝑖+(∑𝑗)𝑉𝑓𝑗ΠLS(𝑗)𝑉𝑗𝑖+(∑𝑗)𝑉𝑓𝑖ΠLS(𝑗)𝑉𝑗𝑘ΠLS(𝑘)𝑉𝑘𝑖+⋯

    Where 𝑇𝑖𝑗=⟨𝜙𝑖|𝑇|𝜙𝑗⟩, 𝑉𝑖𝑗=⟨𝜙𝑖|𝑉|𝜙𝑗⟩, ΠLS(𝑗)=1𝐸−𝐸𝑗 with 𝐸𝑓=𝐸𝑖 and the sums tend to be omitted

  • We can with a certain particle state |𝑖⟩ and end with a final certain particle state |𝑓⟩ and use OFPT to calculate what happens in-between such states. An example of this is the case of an electron scattering off an electron.

Example 3.5.3.1 (Electron Scattering).

This is an example from the textbook that I was reading which allows for the derivation of the Advanced and Retarded propagators.

  • The transition matrix element is

    𝑇𝑓𝑖=𝑉𝑓𝑖+∑𝑛𝑉𝑓𝑛1𝐸𝑖−𝐸𝑛𝑉𝑛𝑖+⋯
  • For electron scattering, the initial and final states are |𝑖⟩=|𝜓𝑒1𝜓𝑒2⟩ and ⟨𝑓|=⟨𝜓𝑒3𝜓𝑒4|
  • Due to the fact that Coulomb’s law is replaced by photon exchange we need a photon field 𝜙(𝑥).

  • This provides

    𝑉=12𝑒∫𝑑3𝑥𝜓𝑒(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥)𝜓𝑒(𝑥)

    with the 12 from spin and the 𝑒 as some coupling constant (which happens to be the electron charge).

    • This interaction turns a 𝑝⃗1 electron into a 𝑝⃗3 electron and a 𝑝⃗𝛾 photon.
    • Since both |𝑖⟩ and |𝑓⟩ have 2 electrons and no photons, 𝑉𝑖𝑗=0
3.5.3.1 Retarded and Advanced Propagators

  • This gets split into two states. (propagated by the Retarded Propagator and the Advanced Propagator)

  • The propagators that this creates are foundational to quantum field theory, (the advanced and retarded ones), which is the primary reason behind this methodology.

  • In the Retarded state, electrons interact via the Retarded Propagator.

  • We have that

    |𝑛⟩=|𝜓𝑒3𝜙𝛾𝜓𝑒2⟩

    • Which implies that

      𝑉𝑛𝑖𝑅=⟨𝜓𝑒3𝜙𝛾𝜓𝑒2|𝑉|𝜓𝑒1𝜓𝑒2⟩=⟨𝜓𝑒3𝜑𝛾|𝑉|𝜓𝑒1⟩⟨𝜓𝑒2|𝜓𝑒2⟩=⟨𝜓𝑒3𝜙𝛾|𝑉|𝜓𝑒1⟩

  • For the advanced state, a similar result is derived

    • 𝑉𝑛𝑖𝐴=⟨𝜓𝑒4𝜑𝛾|𝑉|𝜓𝑒2⟩
3.5.3.2 Evaluating The Propagators
  • 𝑉𝑛𝑖𝑅=⟨𝜓𝑒3𝜑𝛾|𝑉|𝜓𝑒1⟩=𝑒2∫d3𝑥⟨𝜓𝑒3𝜑𝛾|𝜓𝑒(𝑥)𝜙(𝑥)𝜓𝑒(𝑥)|𝜓𝑒1⟩
    • Free field (like the photon and electron fields inside of the integral)
    ⟨𝜙𝛾|𝜙(𝑥)|0⟩=𝑒−𝑖𝑝⃗⋅𝑥⃗

  • This implies:

    𝑉𝑛𝑖𝑅=𝑒∫d3𝑥𝑒𝑖(𝑝⃗1−𝑝⃗2−𝑝⃗3)⋅𝑥⃗=𝑒(2𝜋)3𝛿3(𝑝⃗1−𝑝⃗2−𝑝⃗3)
    • This is similar to other matrix elements

  • First order:

    𝑇𝑓𝑖=∫d3𝑝⃗𝛾(2𝜋)3𝛿3(𝑝⃗1−𝑝⃗2−𝑝⃗𝛾)(2𝜋)3𝛿3(𝑝⃗2−𝑝⃗4+𝑝⃗𝛾)𝑒2𝐸𝑖−𝐸𝑛
    • Energy is not conserved in such intermediate states (otherwise 𝐸𝑖=𝐸𝑛 would blow u
